results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You must keep tax‑related records as long as they may be needed to support any item of income or deduction on a return, or for the period of limitations for that return. In practice that means:

* Keep records that support income, expenses, or deductions on a return until the period of limitations for that return ends. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* For employment taxes, keep all employment‑tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition, so you can compute any depreciation, amortization, depletion, or basis when you sell or otherwise dispose of the property. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* When records are no longer needed for tax purposes, don’t discard them until you confirm that no other purpose (e.g., insurance or creditors) requires a longer retention period. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
Because business records are the evidence that the IRS and other parties rely on to verify what you claim on your returns, to assess your rights and responsibilities, and to keep your business running smoothly. The documents provide the following specific purposes:

* **Support income and deductions on your tax return** – supporting documents prove the amounts reported in your books and on the return. “​It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

* **Enable you to prepare accurate financial statements** – “Good records will help you… prepare your financial statements.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
  “These statements can help you in dealing with your bank or creditors and help you manage your business.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

* **Facilitate audits and inspections** – “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

* **Meet tax‑law retention requirements** – “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
  “For example, if you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Help manage day‑to‑day operations and future planning** – “Good records will help you… monitor the progress of your business.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

Keeping these records in an organized, legible, and secure form is therefore a legal requirement and a practical necessity for any business.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The documents explain the factors that determine which accounting method you should use:

- **If you have no inventory, the cash method is usually the simplest:** “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash method records” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

- **If inventory is necessary, you generally must use the accrual method,** unless you meet the “small‑business” exception and your inventory is treated as non‑incidental material or supplies:  
  *“If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases, unless you are a small business taxpayer…”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
  *“If you account for inventories as materials and supplies that are not incidental, you deduct the amounts paid or incurred to acquire or produce the inventoriable items treated as non‑incidental materials and supplies in the year in which they are first used or consumed in your operations.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).

- **Choosing an accounting method occurs when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C** (Form 1040). If you later want to change methods, you generally need IRS approval (Form 3115) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

So, use the **cash method if you do not carry inventory**; if you carry inventory, use the **accrual method**, unless you qualify for the small‑business inventory exception and treat your inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies, in which case cash may still be acceptable.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To identify and evaluate hazards in your workplace, the OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook recommends a systematic, routine self‑inspection process:

1. **Perform a routine workplace self‑inspection**  
   * “An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the handbooks’ self‑inspection checklists**  
   * “The checklists in the handbook are intended for general industry workplaces, but not for construction or maritime industries. They are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
   * “At the end of each checklist, you will find a link to additional resources on that topic.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Follow the seven‑step program approach**  
   * “The Recommended Practices present a step‑by‑step approach to implementing a successful safety and health program, built around seven core elements: … Hazard identification and assessment … Hazard prevention and control.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

4. **Compile information and track controls**  
   * “Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information … to help you determine where challenges exist.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
   * “Refer to OSHA standards, resources on the OSHA website, and other resources listed in this handbook to find solutions to those challenges.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

5. **Consider additional assistance**  
   * “OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation program can help small‑business employers with this process at no cost.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
   * “OSHA Compliance Assistance Specialists…provide information on OSHA’s compliance assistance resources and cooperative programs.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

6. **Document and review**  
   * “Every workplace should have a safety and health program that includes management leadership, worker participation, and a systematic approach to finding and fixing hazards. Regular workplace inspections are an important tool for identifying hazards and fixing them.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=5)

**Bottom line:**  
Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists to walk through each work area, note any hazards, and record your findings. Cross‑reference those findings with injury/illness records and training logs, then use OSHA resources or an onsite consultant to define control measures and verify their effectiveness. Repeat this process regularly—documenting everything—to maintain a safe, compliant workplace.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 7)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)
3. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 91)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)
4. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=5)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash method vs. Accrual method  

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is counted** | In the year the money is actually received (or deposited). | In the year the income is earned—when the right to receive it is fixed, even if payment comes later. |
| **When expenses can be deducted** | In the year the money is actually paid. | In the year the expense is incurred—when the liability is fixed and economic performance occurs, even if payment is later. |
| **Typical use** | Most sole‐owner and small businesses without inventories. | Businesses that sell or produce inventory, or that want to match income and expenses. |

These rules are set out in IRS Publication 334 (Tax Guide for Small Business):  

- “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it… You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
- “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a deduction for ordinary and necessary **business‑travel** expenses when you are traveling away from your “tax home” for work.  The expenses that can be deducted include transportation, meals, lodging, baggage/shipping, and other costs that are directly related to the business trip (intermediate expenses such as telephone calls, dry‑cleaning, tips, etc. are also deductible).  You may use either actual expenses or the standard meal allowance when calculating the deduction, and usually only 50 % of meal costs are deductible.  The deduction is limited to the portion of the expense that is for business use; the personal portion is not deductible.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is meant to give a concise, one‑to‑two paragraph snapshot of the business plan. It should provide:

* a brief description of the business idea,
* an estimate of the amount of money needed and how it will be used,
* a short statement of the owner’s or owners’ equity contribution, and
* a concise schedule of the business’s goals and milestones.  
It should be written last, after the rest of the plan is complete, so that the summary can reflect the most up‑to‑date information.  

(Executive Summary guidance: “...This portion should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of what you want to accomplish. For example, describe your idea, how much money you need, what you need it for, how much money you will bring (or have put) into the business, and a brief schedule of your goals.” – [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 4])

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, a business plan should:

1. **Identify the niche and the “best” customer** – specify who you are selling to and list the customer’s characteristics.  
   - *Business markets*: “classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.”  
   - *Consumer markets*: “segmented by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought.”  
   – *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

2. **Estimate the size and growth potential** – use population figures, sales‑tax data, industry information, etc., to gauge how much of the total market you can capture.  
   – *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

3. **Explain how you will reach and serve that segment** – detail product/service attributes, distribution, promotion, and pricing that appeal to the target group.  
   – *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)*  

These steps provide the concrete, document‑based approach the SBA handbook recommends for outlining a target market.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  If you own, operate, lease or lease‑to a shop that serves the public, you are a **public accommodation** and the Americans with Disabilities Act requires you to remove “barriers” that are **readily achievable**.  Existing facilities (built before 1993) are not exempt—“existing facilities are not exempted by…grandfather provisions” and must comply with the ADA for new or altered elements, and any reached‑accessible arrangements that can be made without undue expense must be implemented.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

results.question: how many employees before ada employment rules apply
results.answer:
The ADA requires that employment‑related provisions be followed when a business has **15 or more employees**.  
The ADA guide for small businesses states:  

> “The EEOC offers technical assistance on the ADA provisions for employment which apply to businesses with 15 or more employees.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
According to the **OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook**:

*“Employers are partially exempt from OSHA’s injury and illness recordkeeping requirements if 1) they had 10 or fewer workers during all of the last calendar year, or 2) they are in certain low‑hazard industries (see 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A). All employers, regardless of size or industry, must report work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Therefore, you are exempt **only if** your business had 10 or fewer workers *all* of the last calendar year or you operate in one of the OSHA‑listed low‑hazard industries. If neither condition applies, you are **not** exempt and must keep the required injury/illness records.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how long do i keep injury records
results.answer:
Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) must be kept at the worksite for at least five years.  
[osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15]

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Choose a business structure and register it**  
   • Pick the legal form that fits your plans (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation, etc.).  The IRS explains the options and the filing requirements on the first pages of *Publication 583*【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 2】.  
   • If you’ll hire employees, run payroll, or file excise or employment taxes, you must obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  The IRS tells you how to apply for an EIN online, by mail, fax, or phone, and when you need it【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 4】.  

2. **Create a business plan (recommended)**  
   • The SBA’s *Small Business Planning Guide* lays out a step‑by‑step framework: define your business, market, operations, finances, and legal requirements.  See the outline on page 3‑4 of the guide【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 3】【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 4】.  
   • Your plan will be useful when you apply for a loan, file taxes, or manage growth.  

3. **Open a separate business bank account and set up a checkbook**  
   • The IRS recommends keeping business and personal money separate.  The “business checkbook” is the main source for recording expenses and receipts.  It should include deposits, withdrawals, and checks that match your records【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14】.  

4. **Choose an accounting method**  
   • Decide between cash or accrual accounting.  Cash is simpler for many sole proprietors, but if you keep inventory you’ll likely need accrual.  Your method must match how you record income and expenses, and you can’t change it mid‑year without getting approval【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12】.  

5. **Set up a bookkeeping system**  
   • **Single‑entry** – track only a cash basis income statement (daily cash receipts/​pay‑outs).  
   • **Double‑entry** – use journals and ledgers to record every debit and credit, giving you a complete picture of assets, liabilities, and equity.  The guide shows sample journal entries and explains the difference between the two systems【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 15】.  

6. **Keep proper supporting documents**  
   • For every transaction, retain the underlying receipt, invoice, or bank statement that shows the amount, date, and purpose.  The IRS lists the types of documents you should keep for gross receipts, expenses, inventories, and asset depreciation【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12】.  

7. **Record keeping and reconciliation**  
   • Reconcile your bank statement to your checkbook each month; note any missing deposits or outstanding checks so that the balance matches【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14】.  
   • Maintain a summary of all cash receipts and monthly cash disposal records, plus a Check‑Disbursements Journal and an Employee‑Compensation Record if you have staff【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 11】.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your employees safe and your premises accessible you should follow the requirements and recommendations in the two key documents that apply to small businesses:

---

## 1.  Keeping Employees Safe  

| What you must do | Where it is stated |
|------------------|-------------------|
| **Develop a safety‑and‑health program** – identify hazards, conduct inspections, train workers, keep records, and review the program at least annually. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10) |
| **Provide fall protection, personal‑protective equipment (PPE) and respiratory protection** when required by OSHA standards. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=4) |
| **Implement lock‑out/tag‑out procedures** for machinery that can be energized while in service or maintenance. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=50) |
| **Maintain clean, clear walk‑working surfaces** and safe exit routes. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) |
| **Have a whistleblower policy** that protects workers who report safety concerns. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=93) |
| **Report new hires** and keep all employment‑tax records for at least four years. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Carry workers’‑compensation insurance** (often required by state law) and keep it current. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |

---

## 2.  Making Your Premises Accessible (ADA)  

| What you must do | Where it is stated |
|------------------|-------------------|
| **Provide accessible parking** – at least one accessible space for every 25‑50 total spaces; a van‑accessible space if you have only one.  Each space needs a 5‑ft (or 8‑ft for vans) access aisle and a 98‑in clearance. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Create at least one accessible entrance** – a 36‑in wide door or a 32‑in wide door with a lever handle, and an accessible route from the sidewalk to the entrance.  No steps or a maximum 1:12 slope. | (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, pages 10‑11) |
| **Keep all doors and openings** (including power‑door, turnstiles, and automatic doors) accessible if they are part of the main entrance path. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Install accessible sales or service counters** – 36‑in long and no higher than 36‑in above the floor, with a 30×48‑in clear space in front. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Provide accessible aisles and merchandise displays** – a 36‑in wide route, with 3‑ft turning space at corners, and keep shelves at least 3‑ft high so that the clear space is maintained. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Keep signage**: use the international symbol of accessibility on all accessible parking, entrances, exits, and accessible routes. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Review and update policies** – e.g., ensure the accessible entry is not left locked during business hours, allow service animals, and provide multilingual assistance if needed. | [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |

---

### Quick Checklist

1. **Safety Program** – inventory hazards, train staff, keep records.  
2. **PPE & Fall Protection** – staff trained, equipment inspected.  
3. **Lock‑out/Tag‑out** – written procedures, clear labeling.  
4. **Inspections** – walkways, machinery, electrical.  
5. **Employers’ Insurance** – workers’ comp, unemployment, etc.  
6. **ADA Conditions** – parking, entrance, signage, counters, aisles, doors.  
7. **Accessible Signage** – symbol of accessibility on all required places.  
8. **Policy Review** – keep policies inclusive and up‑to‑date.

Following these steps not only protects employees but also makes your business welcoming and compliant with law.

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**How to write a business plan**

1. **Start with a clear outline** – The SBA guide recommends beginning with a cover page, optional table of contents, and an executive summary, then moving into the core sections: Business, Management, Market, and Money.  
   *The SBA guide explains that the outline should “identify the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats that may affect your business and the strategy you will use to succeed.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  

2. **Business section** – Describe the product or service, the industry, and how you will maintain a competitive advantage.  
   *“Describe the overall industry and how your business will maintain a sustainable competitive advantage…Include the regulations that affect the sale and use of your product.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)*  

3. **Management section** – Outline ownership, key personnel, and their responsibilities, and include résumés if possible.  
   *The guide notes that “Describe who is behind the business…also indicate who manages the business on a day‑to‑day basis…If you can’t afford a professional, you may need to reconsider the feasibility of your venture.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)*  

4. **Market section** – Identify your target market, competition, and marketing strategy.  
   *“Describe your market niche; who is your best customer…Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

5. **Money section** – Include financial projections and supporting documents.  
   *The SBA recommends including a “Sources and Uses of Funds” statement, a three‑year income projection, a cash‑flow projection, a balance sheet, and a break‑even analysis [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).*  

6. **Finish with exhibits** – Attach any additional supporting documents (resumes, contracts, product photos, etc.).  
   *“Examples of resumes, purchase agreements, bids, contracts, floor plans, etc.” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)*  

**How to set up accounting**

1. **Choose an accounting method** – The first time you file a business tax return, decide whether to use the cash method or the accrual method.  
   *“An accounting method is a set of rules used to determine when and how income and expenses are reported…You choose an accounting method when you file your first income tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040).” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)*  

2. **Set up a bookkeeping system** –  
   * **Single‑entry** is simple, using a daily summary of cash receipts.  
   * **Double‑entry** tracks all accounts (assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses) and uses journals and ledgers.  
   * “A double‑entry bookkeeping system uses journals and ledgers. Transactions are first entered in a journal and then posted to ledger accounts.” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

3. **Open a dedicated business bank account** – Helps keep business records clean.  
   *“When you start a business, open a business checking account…Use the business account for business purposes only.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*  

4. **Record transactions promptly** – Capture receipts, invoices, and payments as they occur.  
   *“Record expenses when they occur…Generally, it is best to record transactions on a daily basis.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*  

5. **Reconcile monthly** – Compare the bank statement with your ledger to find errors.  
   *“You should reconcile your checking account each month…Verify how much money you have in the account, make sure your checkbook and books reflect all bank charges, and correct any errors.” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)*  

6. **Choose proper tax year** – Most small businesses use the calendar year (Jan 1–Dec 31). If you need a fiscal year, file Form 1128 for approval.  
   *“If you adopt the calendar‑tax year, you must maintain your books and records and report your income and expenses for the period from January 1 through December 31 of each year.” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)*  

7. **Track inventory (if applicable)** – If you sell physical products, keep an inventory and use the accrual method for inventory transactions.  
   *“If you produce, purchase, or sell merchandise…you must keep an inventory and use an accrual method for purchases and sales.” [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)*  

By following the SBA’s business‑plan outline and using the IRS guidelines for selecting a method, recording transactions, and reconciling accounts, you’ll be able to draft a clear, professional business plan and establish a solid accounting foundation for your new venture.

results.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
results.answer:
**What you should track for taxes**

| Category | What to keep | Source |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| **General income and expenses** | Detailed receipts, invoices, and bank statements that show the amount, date, and purpose of every business transaction | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Tax‑related documents** | Copies of all Forms W‑2, W‑3, 1099‑MISC, 1099‑NEC, 8300, and any other information‑return forms you file or receive | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Payroll information** | Employee payroll records, wage statements, and any payroll‑related withholding records | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Estimated tax payments** | Records of all estimated tax payments (dates, amounts, forms 1040‑ES vouchers) | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Business assets** | Purchase invoices, sales receipts, and depreciation schedules for all tangible property | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Tax‑related record‑keeping period** | Retain all records for the period of limitations (the length of time the IRS can assess additional tax or you can amend your return) | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Mileage and travel logs (if you claim business mileage)** | Daily mileage logs that show the date, purpose, business miles driven, and total miles | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |

**What you should track for travel expenses**

| Expense type | What to keep | Source |
|--------------|--------------|--------|
| **Transportation** | Receipts or logs for airfare, train, bus, and rental‑car charges; mileage logs for car travel | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine** | Fares and receipts for transportation between airport/rail‑station and hotel or between hotel and business locations | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Baggage & shipping** | Receipts for shipping baggage, samples, or display materials between home and temporary work sites | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Car or truck expenses** | Detailed mileage logs or actual expenses (gas, oil, tires, insurance, taxes, parking, tolls, lease or loan payments, registration) that are business‑related | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Meals** | Receipts for meals (log the date, location, attendees, business purpose) – only 50 % of the cost is generally deductible | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging** | Hotel receipts showing the date, location, and business purpose of the stay | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Other travel costs** | Receipts for telephone (business calls while away), cleaning, postage, parking (not commuting), and any other incidental travel expenses | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Reimbursement logs** | If reimbursing employees, keep a record of what was paid, the business purpose, and the plan (accountable vs. non‑accountable) | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

**Why record all of this?**  
The IRS requires that you keep supporting documentation for every item you expense. Proper documentation makes it easier to prepare your tax return, claim deductions, and defend the expenses if your records are ever reviewed or examined. The IRS may require you to provide this documentation at any time.  

These are the specific items that the IRS documents mandate you record when you’re tracking taxes and travel expenditures for your business.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
You **do need an EIN** if your business falls into one of the situations where the IRS requires a taxpayer‑identification number other than your SSN.  The documents identify the conditions that trigger an EIN requirement:

- *“You must have a TIN so the IRS can process your returns. Two of the most common kinds of TINs are the social security number (SSN) and the employer identification number (EIN).”*  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

- *“You must have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following:  
  ‑ Pay wages to one or more employees.  
  ‑ File pension or excise tax returns.”*  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

- *“EINs are assigned to sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and other entities by the IRS for tax filing and reporting purposes.”*  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

In short, if you plan to pay employees, file pension or excise returns, or simply want a separate business identification number for banking or credit purposes, you should obtain an EIN.

---

### Accounting method “with” an EIN

An EIN is not directly tied to a particular accounting method.  The method you use is chosen **when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business**.  The documents explain that you can pick one of the standard methods at that time, and future changes normally require IRS approval:

- *“You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business. After that, if you want to change your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval.”*  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

The selectable methods are:

- Cash method  
- Accrual method  
- Special methods for certain items of income and expense  
- Combination method using elements of the above  

(see the “Kinds of methods” section in the same passage).  

So, obtaining an EIN does not dictate a specific accounting method; that choice is made when you prepare your first business tax return.

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
You should keep the OSHA injury and illness records at your worksite and retain them for **at least five years**. The documents you must keep are:

- **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses.  
- **OSHA Form 301** – the Injury and Illness Incident Report (a supplementary record for each recordable case).  
- **OSHA Form 300A** – the annual Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses.  

These records are kept in paper or electronically, but each must be available for inspection by OSHA and must be retained for **five years** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).
